newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Analysts divided on SGB's Tractebel bid.
newsitem.headline: Analysts divided on SGB's Tractebel bid.

text.p: Belgian analysts are divided on whether retail investors should respond to Societe Generale de Belgique's (SGB) bid for utility group Tractebel.
SGB bought 25 percent of Tractebel from holding company Groupe Bruxelles Lambert (GBL) on September 17 and affiliates, boosting its stake in the energy and engineering company to 65 percent.
In order to offer small shareholders the same conditions as GBL, SGB is set to make a 14,500 franc per share public offer for the rest of Tractebel's capital on October 9-30.

But SGB does not have the ambition or the cash to acquire 100 percent of Tractebel. In an effort to dissuade shareholders from selling, it is offering them a put warrant allowing to sell Tractebel stock to SGB at 14,500 francs in three years' time.
Should Tractebel shareholders hold on to their stock or not? Some say yes, some say no.
"Tractebel is an outright sell," said Dewaay, Servais analyst Danny Wittenberg.
Wittenberg said that in light of the upcoming liberalisation of the European electricity market, there was more downside risk than upside potential for the Tractebel group.
He also said Tractebel shares will be weighed down by SGB's desire to re-place with other institutions part of the GBL shares in the coming months.

At the announcement of the operation, SGB said it had preferred buying GBL's block itself rather than see a foreign operator acquire a large minority stake in Tractebel and indicated it may want to re-place some of the Tractebel stock.
Wittenberg saw little financial reason to hold on to Tractebel stock, which has a prospective net dividend yield of about 2.62 percent -- lower than the yield on a bank savings deposit account.
Other analysts were positive about Tractebel stock and advised investors to hold on to their shares.
"I hold on to them, Tractebel is worth more (than the bid price)," said Reyers, Beauvois, Spriet et Cie's Philippe Koeckx.
He said that Tractebel was a well-managed group with a lot of growth potential. "It can only go better," he said, adding that the put warrant protected against downside risk.
But some analysts pointed at a similar operation in January 1994, when German Heidelberger Zement bought a 42 percent stake in cement maker CBR from SGB.

Heidelberger then dissuaded other shareholders from responding to its public bid for CBR by offering a put warrant enabling them to sell CBR shares to Heidelberger in December 1996 at the same price of the January 1994 bid. Since then, CBR shares have been quoted well below that level.
Analysts' Tractebel recommendations are crucial for SGB. If only half of Tractebel's free float is offered to SGB, the company will need to scramble to get more loans.

For the 49 billion francs SGB paid to GBL for the 25 percent Tractebel stake, it only used six billion of its own cash and financed the rest with syndicated loans. Buying the remaining 35 percent of Tractebel would cost another 68 billion francs.

KB Securities analyst Dirk Peeters did not expect SGB would have financial problems if the public responds massively to its Tractebel bid, because Tractebel's dividend yield more than covers the cost of carry for a year.
"SGB has a whole year to replace Tractebel shares," he said.
Analysts said they would be looking for clues about SGB's plans at SGB's first-half 1996 earnings news conference on Tuesday, brought forward by a week because of the Tractebel bid.

Analysts expect no surprises on the earnings front as most of SGB's main holdings have already reported first-half earnings. Group current profit is seen between 6.20 and 6.50 billion francs, from 6.01 billion in the first half of 1995, a rise of four to nine percent. Bottom-line group net profit is seen virtualy stable to three percent above last year's 6.34 billion francs.
-- Geert De Clercq, Brussels Newsroom +32 2 287 6813
